tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

# carma-benchmark

A benchmark is a small, repeatable, runnable experiment that answers one question about the latest changes: **is the data still complete, and is it still fast enough?** It is not the full test plan (that is carma-backend-testing) and not production load. It is the quick check a developer or agent can run after a change and trust.

Read `references/carma-context.md` first for the principles, constraints and spec conventions.

This skill runs outside the main carma flow. It can be used at any time on the current state of the code, with or without specs.

## Inputs

1. **The change.** Find the latest changes (`git diff`, `git log`, or the files the user names). Read the changed code and what it calls.
2. **The specs, if any.** `.specs/architect/` (hot paths HP-n, failure points FP-n, throughput budget), `.specs/data/dba/` (schema, write path), `.specs/testing/backend/` (load profiles and thresholds, so numbers match), `.specs/telemetry/` (counters the benchmark can read), `.specs/devops/` (the Compose stack the benchmark can run against), and the plan in `.specs/plan/` (what the change was meant to deliver).
3. **Existing benchmarks** in `.benchmarks/`. Extend or update them instead of creating near-duplicates.

## Workflow

### 1. Decide what to measure

From the change, choose the question. Usually one of:

- **Completeness** (preferred when in doubt, because a missed mention is the worst failure, P3): every input is accounted for at the end, `received = stored + rejected + quarantined + dead-lettered + duplicate`, text fidelity by hash, planted mentions are all found, nothing stuck "in progress".
- **Performance**: sustained throughput against the 800 articles/sec target, latency percentiles of the changed path, resource cost per article, and freshness from `published_at` to searchable where the path covers it.
- **Both** at once, which is the common case: run at a target rate and verify completeness at the end.

Link each measurement to a failure point or hot path in the specs when they exist, so the benchmark covers what the architect said to watch.

### 2. Check feasibility, and ask when it is not obvious

Not every change can be benchmarked cheaply. Before writing anything, work out which of these applies:

- The change can run in-process with no external services (pure functions, parsing, normalisation, scoring math): easy, benchmark the function directly.
- It needs PostgreSQL: use the Compose stack or a disposable database, with the connection from environment variables. Ask which instance to use and warn that a shared or production database must never be the target.
- It needs an external dependency (an LLM, a source feed): use a fake or stub with controllable latency and failures, and say that the result then measures our code, not the dependency.
- It is a UI, a one-off script, a config change, or has no measurable behaviour: say so and recommend not writing a benchmark, or a different kind of check.

When the approach, the data or a caveat is unclear, **prompt the user before writing code**, using the protocol in the context file (grouped questions, recommended option first, trade-offs in a line). Typical questions:

- What to benchmark: completeness, performance or both, and which path.
- The approach: in-process micro benchmark, against a local database, against the Compose stack, or end to end through the real entry point.
- The data: generated by the bundled generator (default), a sample the user supplies (anonymised), or a captured file; the size and language mix.
- Thresholds: use the agreed 15-minute and 800/s numbers where they apply; ask for the rest or propose values and label them `proposed`.
- Caveats the user accepts: stubbed dependencies, small data volume, hardware not production-like, short duration.

If nobody can answer (unattended run), choose the cheapest approach that answers the question, label each assumption `UNCONFIRMED` in the benchmark's README and in the console output header.

### 3. Design the benchmark

Write down, in the benchmark's README, before the code:

- The question, the change under test and the linked FP/HP entries.
- The approach and what is real versus stubbed.
- The load shape: rate, duration, warm-up, concurrency, seed, language mix, planted mention rate, duplicate and late-arrival rate. Default to a short run (10 to 60 seconds) that gives stable numbers; offer a longer soak as an option rather than the default.
- The metrics reported and each check with its threshold, labelled **agreed** (from the client or an approved spec) or **proposed**.
- How completeness is verified: against the system of record (query the database or ledger), never against the benchmark's own bookkeeping alone.
- Setup, run and clean-up steps, and that the benchmark leaves the target database as it found it (its own schema or marked rows that it removes).

### 4. Write it

Place everything in `.benchmarks/<feature-slug>/`:

- `bench-lib.mjs`: copy from `assets/bench-lib.mjs` (dependency-free, Node 18+). It provides seeded article generation (English, Arabic, Chinese, planted brand mentions, duplicates), a rate-paced load runner with bounded concurrency, latency percentiles, error aggregation, a `Report` with PASS and FAIL checks, a conservation helper and a `main` wrapper. Do not rewrite these; extend through the benchmark script. Improve the copy in the benchmark folder if it is genuinely missing something.
- `bench.mjs`: start from `assets/bench.template.mjs`. Import the code under test, drive the load, verify completeness, and set thresholds.
- `README.md`: the design from step 3 and how to run it.
- `.gitignore` with `results/`, so outputs are not committed.
- Dependencies: use Node's standard library. If the benchmark needs a database driver, use the one the project already depends on, and say so in the README. Do not add heavy tooling for a quick check.

Requirements for every benchmark:

- **Runs with `node .benchmarks/<feature>/bench.mjs [--rate N --duration S --seed N ...]`**, with defaults that work without arguments.
- **Clear errors.** Errors encountered while running are aggregated and printed with counts, a sample context and a short stack, and never swallowed. A benchmark that cannot run (missing environment variable, database unreachable) says what is missing and exits with code 2, distinct from a measured failure.
- **Clear verdict.** The console shows the metrics, a checks table with PASS or FAIL per check and each threshold's origin, and a final `RESULT: PASS` or `RESULT: FAIL` line. Exit code 0 for pass, 1 for fail, 2 for could not run.
- **Reproducible.** A seed, and the environment (Node version, hardware summary, database settings if relevant) printed in the header. Performance numbers without their environment are not comparable.
- **Honest.** Warm-up excluded from the measured window; the achieved rate reported next to the target (if the generator or the harness cannot keep up, that is shown, not hidden); percentiles rather than averages; no threshold chosen so that today's result happens to pass.
- **Safe.** No secrets in the files. Connection details come from environment variables. Refuses to run against a database whose name or host looks like production unless explicitly overridden. Never prints credentials.
- **Cheap to read.** Keep `bench.mjs` short and plain; the harness carries the machinery.

### 5. Run it and report

Run the benchmark at least once if the environment allows, and show the real console output. If it cannot be run here (no database), say so, state what remains to be verified, and do not invent numbers. If it fails, report what failed and whether it points to the change, the benchmark or the environment. When a result looks surprising, run again with a different seed before concluding.

### 6. Feed back into design

Benchmarking often reveals design issues. State them plainly, and raise those that need a decision:

- Code that is hard to benchmark is hard to test and operate. Note where a seam is missing: a function that cannot be called without the whole service, a hidden dependency on the system clock or random source, no way to read how many items were processed.
- Missing counters or ledger states needed to verify completeness (route to carma-telemetry and carma-dba).
- Hot paths that miss budget (route to carma-architect, and to carma-review for readability of that path).
- A needed environment or fixture (route to carma-devops, for a Compose `bench` profile).
- A threshold nobody has agreed (route to the user).

Do not change the architecture silently. Write the findings in the README under "Design implications" and in the reply.

## Output

In the reply: what was benchmarked and why, the approach and caveats, the run command, the real console result or what prevented a run, and the design implications. The artefacts are the files under `.benchmarks/<feature-slug>/`.

## Persisting the work (when run inside a codebase)

The benchmark itself lives in `.benchmarks/<feature-slug>/` as above. If the work leads to a binding decision (for example an agreed threshold), suggest recording it as an ADR through carma-architect. If you are not in a codebase, deliver the files in the conversation and offer to save them.

1	# Carma shared context
2	
3	Every carma-* skill reads this file first. It is the compact form of the "Carma PoC: Core Design Principles" document plus the constraints agreed with the client. When a skill's output has to choose between options, these principles are the tie-breakers, so cite them by number (P1, P6, ...) in specs.
4	
5	## 1. What we are building
6	
7	A proof of concept for Carma, a media intelligence company that aggregates online content (news, social, broadcast, print) and delivers it to PR and communications clients. The PoC is an **internal tool**. Its job is to **prepare data and make it searchable**. Client-facing presentation, export and sharing come later in the pipeline and are out of scope (see "Deferred" below).
8	
9	## 2. Agreed constraints
10	
11	| Area | Decision |
12	| --- | --- |
13	| Backing store | PostgreSQL. Carma's internal limitations rule out an event-driven platform such as Kafka for now. Queues, retries and processing state therefore live in the database or in-process. |
14	| Volume | About 800 articles per second, roughly 69 million a day. Maximise throughput; capacity is measured against this load. |
15	| Latency target | A brand mention reaches a user within 15 minutes of the article's `published_at` time, for every source and language. Insights are delivered daily or weekly and are not held to this target. |
16	| Priority on conflict | Completeness beats speed. A late item is better than a missed one. Items that miss the target are flagged, not dropped. |
17	| Input data | Articles only: `id`, `headline`, `body`, `source`, `published_at` (UTC timestamp), `language`. Other source types are out of scope. |
18	| Content fidelity | The emphasis is on text content. Storing exact, replicable HTML is not a goal. Headline and body are kept as text and are the system of record. Any markup is reduced to text during validation, and the reduction is recorded as a transformation. Raw markup is not retained by default. A hash of the received payload is kept for integrity and dedupe. |
19	| Deployment | Everything runs under Docker Compose on the target machine: database, web app, workers, observability. `docker compose up` on that machine must set everything up automatically (migrations, roles, extensions, secrets, dashboards). Keys and secrets are handled as configuration, never committed. Compose is single-host, so capacity fit against the 800/s target is checked rather than assumed. |
20	| Languages | English, Arabic and Chinese are in scope for the exercise. Nothing may hard-code those three: any language must work through the same data model. |
21	| Confidence scale | One 0 to 100% scale for every derived field. Scorers usually report on 0 to 1 or another range, so a min/max range is supplied per scoring source and values are normalised. |
22	| Fields needing confidence | Sentiment, relevance, topic, summary, entity match. |
23	| Calibration | Out of scope. Transparency (P7) lets a human or agent decide whether a value is acceptable. |
24	| Evidence base | Carma's public website only. Carma is assumed to agree with the principles. |
25	
26	Illustrative sizing, to be replaced by measurement: 800/s is 48,000 a minute and 2.88 million an hour. The 15-minute window therefore holds about 720,000 articles in flight. At 1 ms of CPU per article the pipeline needs 0.8 cores, at 10 ms it needs 8, at 100 ms it needs 80, so per-article cost is the first thing to question. At 1 to 5 KB of text per article, raw storage is roughly 69 to 345 GB a day before indexes and WAL, so retention and partitioning are first-order design concerns.
27	
28	The sample article in the brief is about 500 characters, shorter than a typical real article. Treat it as a schema example, not a size benchmark.
29	
30	## 3. Principles
31	
32	Use these as design tests: "which principle does this choice serve, and which does it cost?"
33	
34	| # | Principle | In one line | Ask yourself |
35	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
36	| P1 | Fast | Published to visible with minimal delay; clock starts at `published_at` | Is capture lag measured separately from processing time? Can fresh items be searchable before enrichment finishes? |
37	| P2 | Reliable | Predictable; failures are never silent | What happens on crash, retry, duplicate delivery, backlog? Is processing state recorded so work can resume? |
38	| P3 | Complete, honest about gaps | Broad coverage; what is not covered is visible | Can a user tell "no results" from "not covered" from "not yet processed"? Does any path drop an item? |
39	| P4 | Signal over volume | Noise is a defect | Are dedupe/filter/rank decisions recorded so removed content is recoverable? |
40	| P5 | Consistent across markets and languages | Same data model and field definitions everywhere | Does anything assume Latin script, spaces between words, or left-to-right text? |
41	| P6 | Every insight carries a confidence | 0 to 100% on every derived field, visible by default | Does every derived field have a confidence, or an explicit "no confidence available"? |
42	| P7 | Confidence is inspectable | Origin and method stated plainly, even if unimpressive | Do we store origin, method, inputs, raw value, min/max range and normalised value? |
43	| P8 | Everything traces to its source | Any item can be followed back to the original content | Does each derived item reference its source items and the processing applied? |
44	| P9 | Human judgment is part of the system | Automation and people have defined, visible roles | Where can an analyst review, correct or override? Is output marked automated, human-reviewed or human-authored? |

# Carma shared context

Every carma-* skill reads this file first. It is the compact form of the "Carma PoC: Core Design Principles" document plus the constraints agreed with the client. When a skill's output has to choose between options, these principles are the tie-breakers, so cite them by number (P1, P6, ...) in specs.

## 1. What we are building

A proof of concept for Carma, a media intelligence company that aggregates online content (news, social, broadcast, print) and delivers it to PR and communications clients. The PoC is an **internal tool**. Its job is to **prepare data and make it searchable**. Client-facing presentation, export and sharing come later in the pipeline and are out of scope (see "Deferred" below).

## 2. Agreed constraints

| Area | Decision |
| --- | --- |
| Backing store | PostgreSQL. Carma's internal limitations rule out an event-driven platform such as Kafka for now. Queues, retries and processing state therefore live in the database or in-process. |
| Volume | About 800 articles per second, roughly 69 million a day. Maximise throughput; capacity is measured against this load. |
| Latency target | A brand mention reaches a user within 15 minutes of the article's `published_at` time, for every source and language. Insights are delivered daily or weekly and are not held to this target. |
| Priority on conflict | Completeness beats speed. A late item is better than a missed one. Items that miss the target are flagged, not dropped. |
| Input data | Articles only: `id`, `headline`, `body`, `source`, `published_at` (UTC timestamp), `language`. Other source types are out of scope. |
| Content fidelity | The emphasis is on text content. Storing exact, replicable HTML is not a goal. Headline and body are kept as text and are the system of record. Any markup is reduced to text during validation, and the reduction is recorded as a transformation. Raw markup is not retained by default. A hash of the received payload is kept for integrity and dedupe. |
| Deployment | Everything runs under Docker Compose on the target machine: database, web app, workers, observability. `docker compose up` on that machine must set everything up automatically (migrations, roles, extensions, secrets, dashboards). Keys and secrets are handled as configuration, never committed. Compose is single-host, so capacity fit against the 800/s target is checked rather than assumed. |
| Languages | English, Arabic and Chinese are in scope for the exercise. Nothing may hard-code those three: any language must work through the same data model. |
| Confidence scale | One 0 to 100% scale for every derived field. Scorers usually report on 0 to 1 or another range, so a min/max range is supplied per scoring source and values are normalised. |
| Fields needing confidence | Sentiment, relevance, topic, summary, entity match. |
| Calibration | Out of scope. Transparency (P7) lets a human or agent decide whether a value is acceptable. |
| Evidence base | Carma's public website only. Carma is assumed to agree with the principles. |

Illustrative sizing, to be replaced by measurement: 800/s is 48,000 a minute and 2.88 million an hour. The 15-minute window therefore holds about 720,000 articles in flight. At 1 ms of CPU per article the pipeline needs 0.8 cores, at 10 ms it needs 8, at 100 ms it needs 80, so per-article cost is the first thing to question. At 1 to 5 KB of text per article, raw storage is roughly 69 to 345 GB a day before indexes and WAL, so retention and partitioning are first-order design concerns.

The sample article in the brief is about 500 characters, shorter than a typical real article. Treat it as a schema example, not a size benchmark.

## 3. Principles

Use these as design tests: "which principle does this choice serve, and which does it cost?"

| # | Principle | In one line | Ask yourself |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P1 | Fast | Published to visible with minimal delay; clock starts at `published_at` | Is capture lag measured separately from processing time? Can fresh items be searchable before enrichment finishes? |
| P2 | Reliable | Predictable; failures are never silent | What happens on crash, retry, duplicate delivery, backlog? Is processing state recorded so work can resume? |
| P3 | Complete, honest about gaps | Broad coverage; what is not covered is visible | Can a user tell "no results" from "not covered" from "not yet processed"? Does any path drop an item? |
| P4 | Signal over volume | Noise is a defect | Are dedupe/filter/rank decisions recorded so removed content is recoverable? |
| P5 | Consistent across markets and languages | Same data model and field definitions everywhere | Does anything assume Latin script, spaces between words, or left-to-right text? |
| P6 | Every insight carries a confidence | 0 to 100% on every derived field, visible by default | Does every derived field have a confidence, or an explicit "no confidence available"? |
| P7 | Confidence is inspectable | Origin and method stated plainly, even if unimpressive | Do we store origin, method, inputs, raw value, min/max range and normalised value? |
| P8 | Everything traces to its source | Any item can be followed back to the original content | Does each derived item reference its source items and the processing applied? |
| P9 | Human judgment is part of the system | Automation and people have defined, visible roles | Where can an analyst review, correct or override? Is output marked automated, human-reviewed or human-authored? |
| P10 | Data leads to meaning | Explain what happened and why it matters | Does the data model carry the context needed for explanation (topic, entities, sentiment, relationships)? |
| P11 | Fit the audience | Content suits the person and situation | Can urgency, audience and market be filtered and derived later? |

Every derived value stores: the normalised confidence (0 to 100), the raw score, the min/max range of the scoring source, the origin type, the method and its version, and when it was produced. A 60 from a model's self-report and a 60 from a classifier mean different things, so the origin always travels with the number. Never present a self-reported LLM figure as a statistical probability.

### Deferred (do not design for now)

Shareable-by-default outputs: executive briefings, branded newsletters, ready-made reports, exports. Keep data models from making these harder later (P11), nothing more.

## 4. Known unknowns

- `published_at` is source-supplied and assumed accurate. Missing, future-dated or wrong values would corrupt the 15-minute clock.
- Whether `id` is globally unique or only unique per source.

| --- | --- |
| carma-architect (raw design docs) | `.specs/architect/` |

| carma-searchability | `.specs/search/` |
| carma-telemetry | `.specs/telemetry/` |
| carma-data-sanity | `.specs/data/sanitization/` |
| carma-dba | `.specs/data/dba/` |
| carma-backend-testing | `.specs/testing/backend/` |
| carma-devops | `.specs/devops/` |
| carma-ux | `.specs/ux/` |
| carma-review (runs outside the main flow) | `.specs/review/` |
| carma-benchmark (runs outside the main flow) | `.benchmarks/<feature>/` (executable Node.js files, not numbered specs) |
| carma-plan | `.specs/plan/` |

**"In a codebase" means** the working directory is a project: it has a `.git` directory or a recognisable manifest (`package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod`, `pom.xml`, `Cargo.toml`, `*.csproj`, etc.) or a source tree. If it is not, do not create files. Deliver the output in the conversation and offer to save it once a project is available.

**Numbering.** Each directory has its own sequence of four-digit numbers: `0001-short-slug.md`, `0002-...`. Get the next number with `scripts/next_spec_number.py <directory>`, which also creates the directory if it is missing. Never reuse or renumber a file. Edit a spec in place while its status is `draft`; once it is `approved`, a change is a new file whose front matter says `supersedes`.

**Front matter** on every spec:

```yaml
---
spec: carma-dba            # skill that produced it
number: 0003
title: Partitioned storage for article ingestion
status: draft              # draft | in-review | approved | superseded
date: 2026-10-24
feature: article-ingestion # short name shared across the specs for one feature
inputs: [.specs/architect/0002-article-ingestion.md]
principles: [P1, P2, P3]
supersedes: null
---
```

**Finding inputs.** Upstream specs for the same `feature` are the input. List the relevant directory, read the highest-numbered non-superseded spec for that feature (plus any ADRs that reference it), and record the paths under `inputs`. If an expected input is missing, say so and either run the upstream skill's analysis inline or ask the user, rather than guessing.

## 6. When to ask the user

Ask when a requirement is ambiguous, when two priorities conflict and the principles above do not settle it, or when a choice is expensive to reverse. Do not ask what the constraints above already answer, and do not ask what you can find by reading the codebase.

Ask with the AskUserQuestion tool when it is available (one to four questions, two to four options each, recommended option first and marked). Each option needs its trade-off in one line: what it gains, what it costs, which principles it touches. If the tool is not available, ask in plain text with the same structure. If nobody is available to answer (an unattended or scheduled run), pick the option that best matches the principles, mark it `UNCONFIRMED` in the spec, and list it under open questions so it is not mistaken for a decision.

Group questions: one round of well-formed questions beats a stream of single ones.

65	- Target machine specs (CPU, memory, disk, OS), whether it has internet access to pull images, and whether images are built in CI or on the target.
66	- Real average article size, source mix and language mix.
67	- PostgreSQL version, hosting model and which extensions are permitted in Carma's environment.
68	- Which brand or query sets drive "brand mention" detection, and how many standing queries exist.
69	
70	## 5. Spec conventions (when run inside a codebase)
71	
72	Skills write their output as numbered markdown files so decisions and reasoning survive the conversation and later skills can read them.
73	
74	| Skill | Output directory |
75	| --- | --- |
76	| carma-architect (raw design docs) | `.specs/architect/` |
77	| carma-architect (approved decisions) | `.specs/architect/adrs/` |
78	| carma-searchability | `.specs/search/` |
79	| carma-telemetry | `.specs/telemetry/` |
80	| carma-data-sanity | `.specs/data/sanitization/` |
81	| carma-dba | `.specs/data/dba/` |
82	| carma-backend-testing | `.specs/testing/backend/` |
83	| carma-devops | `.specs/devops/` |
84	| carma-ux | `.specs/ux/` |
85	| carma-review (runs outside the main flow) | `.specs/review/` |
86	| carma-benchmark (runs outside the main flow) | `.benchmarks/<feature>/` (executable Node.js files, not numbered specs) |
87	| carma-plan | `.specs/plan/` |
88	
89	**"In a codebase" means** the working directory is a project: it has a `.git` directory or a recognisable manifest (`package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod`, `pom.xml`, `Cargo.toml`, `*.csproj`, etc.) or a source tree. If it is not, do not create files. Deliver the output in the conversation and offer to save it once a project is available.
90	
91	**Numbering.** Each directory has its own sequence of four-digit numbers: `0001-short-slug.md`, `0002-...`. Get the next number with `scripts/next_spec_number.py <directory>`, which also creates the directory if it is missing. Never reuse or renumber a file. Edit a spec in place while its status is `draft`; once it is `approved`, a change is a new file whose front matter says `supersedes`.
92	
93	**Front matter** on every spec:
94	
95	```yaml
96	---
97	spec: carma-dba            # skill that produced it
98	number: 0003
99	title: Partitioned storage for article ingestion
100	status: draft              # draft | in-review | approved | superseded
101	date: 2026-10-24
102	feature: article-ingestion # short name shared across the specs for one feature
103	inputs: [.specs/architect/0002-article-ingestion.md]
104	principles: [P1, P2, P3]
105	supersedes: null
106	---
107	```
108	
109	**Finding inputs.** Upstream specs for the same `feature` are the input. List the relevant directory, read the highest-numbered non-superseded spec for that feature (plus any ADRs that reference it), and record the paths under `inputs`. If an expected input is missing, say so and either run the upstream skill's analysis inline or ask the user, rather than guessing.
110	
111	## 6. When to ask the user
112	
113	Ask when a requirement is ambiguous, when two priorities conflict and the principles above do not settle it, or when a choice is expensive to reverse. Do not ask what the constraints above already answer, and do not ask what you can find by reading the codebase.
114	
115	Ask with the AskUserQuestion tool when it is available (one to four questions, two to four options each, recommended option first and marked). Each option needs its trade-off in one line: what it gains, what it costs, which principles it touches. If the tool is not available, ask in plain text with the same structure. If nobody is available to answer (an unattended or scheduled run), pick the option that best matches the principles, mark it `UNCONFIRMED` in the spec, and list it under open questions so it is not mistaken for a decision.
116	
117	Group questions: one round of well-formed questions beats a stream of single ones.

1	-- Media Signal Service initial schema
2	-- Rollback (manual): DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE; CREATE SCHEMA public;
3	-- Prefer: docker compose down -v
4	
5	DO $$
6	BEGIN
7	  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'app_ingest') THEN
8	    CREATE ROLE app_ingest LOGIN;
9	  END IF;
10	  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'app_worker') THEN
11	    CREATE ROLE app_worker LOGIN;
12	  END IF;
13	  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'app_read') THEN
14	    CREATE ROLE app_read LOGIN;
15	  END IF;
16	END $$;
17	
18	CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION set_role_password(role_name text, pwd text)
19	RETURNS void
20	LANGUAGE plpgsql
21	AS $$
22	BEGIN
23	  EXECUTE format('ALTER ROLE %I PASSWORD %L', role_name, pwd);
24	END;
25	$$;
26	
27	CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
28	CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS unaccent;
29	CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;
30	
31	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS articles (
32	  id               bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
33	  external_id      text        NOT NULL,
34	  source           text        NOT NULL,
35	  published_at     timestamptz NOT NULL,
36	  ingested_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
37	  language         text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'und',
38	  headline         text,
39	  body             text,
40	  content_hash     bytea       NOT NULL,
41	  flags            text[]      NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
42	  search_text      text        NOT NULL,
43	  search_text_ver  smallint    NOT NULL,
44	  search_vector    tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('simple', search_text)) STORED,
45	  CONSTRAINT articles_has_text CHECK (headline IS NOT NULL OR body IS NOT NULL),
46	  CONSTRAINT articles_source_ext_uq UNIQUE (source, external_id)
47	);
48	
49	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS enrichment_jobs (
50	  id                bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
51	  article_id        bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES articles(id),
52	  part              text   NOT NULL CHECK (part IN ('sentiment','summary_topics')),
53	  prompt_version    text   NOT NULL,
54	  state             text   NOT NULL DEFAULT 'queued'
55	                    CHECK (state IN ('queued','running','succeeded','failed_retryable',
56	                                     'deferred_budget','skipped_no_content','dead')),
57	  attempts          smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
58	  invalid_attempts  smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
59	  next_attempt_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
60	  claimed_by        text,
61	  claimed_at        timestamptz,
62	  claim_expires_at  timestamptz,
63	  reserved_micro    bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
64	  reason_code       text,
65	  last_error        text,
66	  created_at        timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
67	  updated_at        timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
68	  UNIQUE (article_id, part, prompt_version)
69	) WITH (fillfactor = 80);
70	
71	ALTER TABLE enrichment_jobs SET (
72	  autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02
73	);
74	
75	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS enrichments (
76	  id               bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
77	  article_id       bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES articles(id),
78	  part             text   NOT NULL CHECK (part IN ('sentiment','summary_topics')),
79	  provider         text   NOT NULL,
80	  model            text   NOT NULL,
81	  model_reported   text,
82	  prompt_version   text   NOT NULL,
83	  origin           text   NOT NULL CHECK (origin IN ('provider','cache','mock')),
84	  input_hash       bytea  NOT NULL,
85	  input_truncated  boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
86	  input_tokens     integer,
87	  output_tokens    integer,
88	  cost_micro       bigint,
89	  trust            text   NOT NULL DEFAULT 'normal' CHECK (trust IN ('normal','low')),
90	  raw_output       jsonb,
91	  job_id           bigint REFERENCES enrichment_jobs(id),
92	  created_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
93	  superseded_at    timestamptz
94	);
95	CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS enrichments_current_uq
96	  ON enrichments (article_id, part) WHERE superseded_at IS NULL;
97	
98	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS derived_values (
99	  id                bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
100	  enrichment_id     bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES enrichments(id),
101	  article_id        bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES articles(id),
102	  field             text   NOT NULL CHECK (field IN ('sentiment','summary','topic')),
103	  value             text   NOT NULL,
104	  rank              smallint,
105	  vocab_version     smallint,
106	  confidence_norm   numeric(5,2) CHECK (confidence_norm BETWEEN 0 AND 100),
107	  confidence_raw    double precision,
108	  scale_min         double precision,
109	  scale_max         double precision,
110	  confidence_origin text   NOT NULL CHECK (confidence_origin IN
111	                      ('classifier_concentration','llm_self_report','none','mock','human')),
112	  method            text   NOT NULL,
113	  extra             jsonb,
114	  is_current        boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
115	  CONSTRAINT dv_conf_complete CHECK (
116	    (confidence_norm IS NULL AND confidence_origin = 'none')
117	    OR (confidence_norm IS NOT NULL AND confidence_raw IS NOT NULL
118	        AND scale_min IS NOT NULL AND scale_max IS NOT NULL AND scale_min < scale_max))
119	);
120	
121	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS llm_budget_ledger (
122	  provider       text   NOT NULL,
123	  day_utc        date   NOT NULL,
124	  currency       text   NOT NULL,
125	  cap_micro      bigint NOT NULL,
126	  reserved_micro bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
127	  spent_micro    bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
128	  PRIMARY KEY (provider, day_utc),
129	  CHECK (reserved_micro >= 0 AND spent_micro >= 0)
130	);
131	
132	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS system_flags (
133	  key text PRIMARY KEY,
134	  value text NOT NULL,
135	  updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
136	);
137	
138	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ingest_events (
139	  id             bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
140	  batch_id       uuid   NOT NULL,
141	  batch_kind     text   NOT NULL DEFAULT 'backfill' CHECK (batch_kind IN ('live','backfill')),
142	  position       integer NOT NULL,
143	  received_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
144	  payload_sha256 bytea  NOT NULL,
145	  byte_size      integer NOT NULL,
146	  outcome        text   NOT NULL CHECK (outcome IN ('admitted','quarantined','duplicate')),
147	  reason_codes   text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
148	  article_id     bigint REFERENCES articles(id)
149	);
150	
151	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ingest_quarantine (
152	  event_id   bigint PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES ingest_events(id),
153	  reason_codes text[] NOT NULL,
154	  field_errors jsonb,
155	  payload_text text,
156	  status     text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open' CHECK (status IN ('open','replayed','discarded')),
157	  resolved_at timestamptz,
158	  note text,
159	  replayed_article_id bigint REFERENCES articles(id)
160	);
161	
162	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ingest_transformations (
163	  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
164	  article_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES articles(id),
165	  field text NOT NULL,
166	  kind text NOT NULL,
167	  detail jsonb,
168	  tool text NOT NULL,
169	  tool_version text NOT NULL,
170	  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
171	);
172	
173	CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS articles_keyset_idx ON articles (published_at DESC, id DESC);
174	CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS articles_source_keyset_idx ON articles (source, published_at DESC, id DESC);
175	CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS articles_lang_keyset_idx ON articles (language, published_at DESC, id DESC);
176	CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS articles_fts_idx ON articles USING GIN (search_vector);
177	CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS articles_hash_idx ON articles (content_hash);
178	
179	DO $$
180	BEGIN
181	  BEGIN
182	    CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS articles_trgm_idx ON articles USING GIN (search_text gin_trgm_ops);
183	    INSERT INTO system_flags (key, value) VALUES ('trgm_index', 'on')
184	      ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET value = EXCLUDED.value, updated_at = now();
185	  EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN
186	    INSERT INTO system_flags (key, value) VALUES ('trgm_index', 'off')
187	      ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET value = EXCLUDED.value, updated_at = now();
188	  END;
189	END $$;
190	
191	CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS jobs_claim_idx ON enrichment_jobs (part, next_attempt_at, id)
192	  WHERE state IN ('queued','failed_retryable','deferred_budget');
193	CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS jobs_running_idx ON enrichment_jobs (claim_expires_at)
194	  WHERE state = 'running';
195	CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS jobs_article_idx ON enrichment_jobs (article_id, part);
196	CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS dv_article_idx ON derived_values (article_id) WHERE is_current;
197	CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS dv_sentiment_idx ON derived_values (value, article_id)
198	  WHERE field = 'sentiment' AND is_current;
199	CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS dv_topic_idx ON derived_values (value, article_id)
200	  WHERE field = 'topic' AND is_current;
201	CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS events_batch_idx ON ingest_events (batch_id, position);
202	CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS events_hash_idx ON ingest_events (payload_sha256);
203	CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS transf_article_idx ON ingest_transformations (article_id);
204	
205	CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION worker_set_flag(p_key text, p_value text)
206	RETURNS void
207	LANGUAGE plpgsql
208	SECURITY DEFINER
209	SET search_path = public
210	AS $$
211	BEGIN
212	  IF p_key NOT LIKE 'worker.%' AND p_key NOT LIKE 'breaker.%' THEN
213	    RAISE EXCEPTION 'app_worker may only write worker.* or breaker.* flags';
214	  END IF;
215	  INSERT INTO system_flags (key, value, updated_at)
216	  VALUES (p_key, p_value, now())
217	  ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET value = EXCLUDED.value, updated_at = now();
218	END;
219	$$;
220	
221	REVOKE ALL ON FUNCTION worker_set_flag(text, text) FROM PUBLIC;
222	GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION worker_set_flag(text, text) TO app_worker;
223	
224	GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO app_ingest, app_worker, app_read;
225	
226	GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON articles TO app_ingest;
227	GRANT SELECT ON articles TO app_worker, app_read;
228	GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA public TO app_ingest, app_worker;
229

231	GRANT SELECT ON ingest_events TO app_ingest;
232	GRANT SELECT ON ingest_transformations TO app_read;
233	
234	GRANT SELECT ON enrichment_jobs TO app_worker, app_read;
235	GRANT UPDATE ON enrichment_jobs TO app_worker;
236	
237	GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON enrichments TO app_worker;
238	GRANT UPDATE (superseded_at) ON enrichments TO app_worker;
239	GRANT SELECT ON enrichments TO app_read;
240	
241	GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON derived_values TO app_worker;
242	GRANT UPDATE (is_current) ON derived_values TO app_worker;
243	GRANT SELECT ON derived_values TO app_read;
244	
245	GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON llm_budget_ledger TO app_worker;
246	GRANT SELECT ON llm_budget_ledger TO app_read;
247

249

251

function readOptionalFile(path: string | undefined): string | undefined {
  if (!path) return undefined;
  try {
    return readFileSync(path, "utf8").trim();
  } catch {
    return undefined;
  }
}

function envOrFile(name: string, fileName?: string): string | undefined {
  const direct = process.env[name];
  if (direct !== undefined && direct !== "") return direct;
  const fileEnv = fileName ?? `${name}_FILE`;
  return readOptionalFile(process.env[fileEnv]);
}

function readOptionalFile(path: string | undefined): string | undefined {
  if (!path) return undefined;
  try {
    return readFileSync(path, "utf8").trim();
  } catch {
    return undefined;
  }
}

function envOrFile(name: string, fileName?: string): string | undefined {
  const direct = process.env[name];
  if (direct !== undefined && direct !== "") return direct;
  const fileEnv = fileName ?? `${name}_FILE`;
  return readOptionalFile(process.env[fileEnv]);
}

# Benchmark: article ingest (`loadArticles`)

**Question.** Does the initial ingest path keep every article accounted for, and how fast is it, measured against the 800 articles/s target?

**Change under test.** `src/lib/ingest/ingest.ts` (`loadArticles` -> validate, reduce markup, normalise, insert `articles`, `ingest_events`, `ingest_transformations`, `enrichment_jobs`, quarantine). Specs: INV-1 to INV-7 and M-THRU-1 (`.specs/testing/backend/0001`), HP-DB1 (batch insert), HP-5 (sanitiser).

## Approach (what is real, what is stubbed)

- Real: `loadArticles` itself, the real migrations, real PostgreSQL 16.6, the `app_ingest` role (so grants are exercised), the validator, sanitiser and normaliser.
- Stubbed: nothing. Enrichment is not run; only the two queued `enrichment_jobs` rows per article are checked.
- Database: the script creates its own database (`bench_ingest_<random>`) on a **disposable** Postgres, migrates it, and drops it at the end (`--keepDb` to inspect). It refuses non-local hosts unless `BENCH_ALLOW_REMOTE=1`. Migrations create the cluster-level roles `app_ingest`, `app_worker`, `app_read`, which are left behind; use a throwaway cluster.
- Driver: `pg`, already a project dependency. TypeScript is loaded with `tsx` (also already a dependency).

## Load shape

| Setting | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Target rate | 800 articles/s | the agreed Carma target; use `--rate` for others |
| Duration / warm-up | 20 s / 3 s | warm-up excluded from latency and rate |
| Unit of work | batch of 20 (`--batch`) | one `loadArticles` call per batch, up to 16 in flight (`--concurrency`) |
| Seed | 42 | same seed gives the same corpus |
| Corpus | the 20 sample articles used as templates | bodies repeated 1-8x (about 0.4-3 KB), unique ref per article; English, Arabic, Chinese as in the sample |
| Mix | 5% planted token, 1% invalid (quarantine), 1% redelivery (same id), 2% content duplicate (new id), 5% injected markup | `--planted --invalid --redelivery --contentDup --markup` |

Maximum capacity: `--rate 5000` (the rate check then fails by design; read the achieved rate).

## Completeness checks (against the database, not the benchmark's counters)

All labelled **agreed** (INV-1 conservation and related invariants):

1. `received == admitted + quarantined + duplicate` (from `ingest_events`)
2. `count(articles) == admitted events`, and equals the expected number of unique valid (source, id) pairs
3. quarantined events equal the invalid items sent; `ingest_quarantine` rows match
4. no admitted event without an article; every article has exactly 2 `enrichment_jobs`
5. every planted token is found through the `search_vector` index in its own article
6. plain-text bodies are stored byte-identical (sha256)
7. every article with injected markup has an `ingest_transformations` row

Performance checks: achieved rate >= 95% of target (agreed when the target is 800, otherwise proposed), batch p95 <= 2000 ms (**proposed**), zero errors (proposed).

## Run

```bash
docker run -d --rm --name carma-bench-db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=bench -e POSTGRES_USER=bench_admin -e POSTGRES_DB=bench_boot -p 127.0.0.1:54399:5432 --shm-size=256m postgres:16.6-bookworm -c shared_preload_libraries=pg_stat_statements -c shared_buffers=512MB -c max_connections=50 -c wal_compression=on
```

```bash
BENCH_DB_ADMIN_USER=bench_admin BENCH_DB_ADMIN_PASSWORD=bench node --import tsx .benchmarks/article-ingest/bench.mjs
```

Options: `--rate --duration --warmup --concurrency --batch --seed --keepDb`. Env: `BENCH_DB_HOST` (default 127.0.0.1), `BENCH_DB_PORT` (default 54399), `BENCH_DB_ADMIN_USER`, `BENCH_DB_ADMIN_PASSWORD`. Exit code 0 pass, 1 fail, 2 could not run. Stop the database with `docker stop carma-bench-db`.

## Caveats (UNCONFIRMED: not yet agreed with the owner)

- Docker Desktop on Windows, one Postgres container on the same machine as the load generator. Not production-like; numbers are comparable only on the same host.
- Postgres tuning is a modest guess, not `db/postgres/*.conf`.
- Small data volume (about 17,000 rows). Index and autovacuum behaviour at tens of millions of rows is not tested.
- Batch size 20 is a choice; real callers may send one at a time (see design implications).
- Table size and WAL per article are indicative only (WAL is the LSN delta over the run, including index maintenance).

## Design implications

- `ingestOne` is not exported and every article costs 4 or more round trips and its own transaction with a checked-out connection. Throughput is bound by the number of connections: 8 connections gave about 740/s, 16 about 1,075/s. Reaching 800/s needs roughly 16 connections here, which is a lot for a 50-connection limit shared with web and worker. A multi-row or `unnest` insert per batch would be the first thing to try (route to carma-dba / carma-architect).
- `loadArticles` processes a batch serially, so a caller that sends one big batch gets no concurrency at all; the benchmark gets its parallelism by calling it from several chunks. If the real entry point is meant to be a bulk path, say so.
- There is a per-article `SELECT ... WHERE content_hash` for the duplicate flag before the insert; it is cheap now and grows with the table (index on `content_hash` is present).
- `loadArticles` returns counts but not timings. Per-stage timing (validate, reduce, insert) is not available, so this benchmark cannot say where the 8 ms per article goes (route to carma-telemetry).
- The sanitiser collapses whitespace in plain text (the benchmark first tripped on this). That is a transformation of text content; confirm it is recorded in `ingest_transformations` or accepted as normalisation.

I wrote a benchmark for the initial ingest in `.benchmarks/article-ingest/`. At the default 800 articles/s target it passes all 13 checks.

**What it does.** It calls the real `loadArticles` against a throwaway Postgres 16.6 container, `carma-bench-db`, so the running app database is never touched. It uses your 20 sample articles as templates (English, Arabic and Chinese). Bodies are repeated to roughly 0.4–3 KB. Each run mixes in these cases:
- 1% invalid items, which should be quarantined
- 1% redeliveries of the same id
- 2% content duplicates under new ids
- 5% injected markup
- 5% planted search tokens

Completeness is checked in the database, not in the benchmark's own counters:
- received equals admitted plus quarantined plus duplicate
- every article has exactly 2 `enrichment_jobs` rows
- every planted token is found through search
- plain-text bodies are stored byte-identical
- every article with injected markup has a transformation row

**Default run** (800 articles/s target, batch of 20, 16 concurrent, 20 s, seed 42):

| Metric | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Throughput | 794 articles/s |
| Batch p50 / p95 / p99 | 206 / 267 / 333 ms |
| Cost per article | about 10 ms |
| Rows | 18,400 received; 18,016 admitted, 195 quarantined, 189 duplicate |

**Ceiling.** At 8 connections the ceiling was about 740/s. At 16 it was about 1,075/s. An earlier default of 8 connections failed the rate check, so I raised the default to 16.

**Design implications** (also in the README):
- Every article is its own transaction with 4 or more round trips, so throughput is bound by the number of connections. 800/s needs about 16 here, a lot against a 50-connection limit shared with web and worker. A batched insert would be the first thing to try.
- `loadArticles` processes a batch serially, so a single large batch gets no parallelism. The benchmark gets concurrency by calling it from several chunks.
- It reports no per-stage timings, so the roughly 10 ms per article can't be split into validate, sanitise and insert.
- The sanitiser appears to collapse whitespace in plain text. I haven't confirmed whether that is recorded as a transformation, so please check it.

**Caveats.**
- The test ran on Docker Desktop on the same Windows machine, with a modest Postgres tuning and only about 18k rows. I labelled these assumptions UNCONFIRMED in the README.
- The 2000 ms p95 latency threshold is my proposal. The 800/s rate target is the agreed one.
- Nothing is committed.
- The `carma-bench-db` container is still running (`docker stop carma-bench-db` to stop it).

To run it, start the container with the `docker run` command in the README, then:

```bash
BENCH_DB_ADMIN_USER=bench_admin BENCH_DB_ADMIN_PASSWORD=bench node --import tsx .benchmarks/article-ingest/bench.mjs
```
